analysis.one_liner: Lets the Defense Secretary block Freedom of Information Act release of photos of detainee treatment for renewable three-year periods.
analysis.headline: The bill shielding detainee-treatment photos from FOIA passed the Senate the day it was introduced but died in House committees without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let the Secretary of Defense certify photographs of the treatment of detainees captured after September 11, 2001 — including Abu Ghraib-era images — as too dangerous to release, taking them out of reach of Freedom of Information Act requests and court challenges. Each certification would last three years and could be renewed indefinitely. The decision would rest solely with the Defense Secretary, checked only by a notice to Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: The Defense Department and the intelligence community gain a permanent legal shield for photographs documenting the treatment of detainees held by U.S. forces, since certifications can be renewed every three years without limit. The government also retains full discretion to release photos voluntarily on its own schedule.

how_it_helps.text: It gives the Defense Secretary authority to exempt photographs of detainee treatment from all FOIA disclosure if he determines release would endanger Americans, troops, or government employees abroad.
It blocks any court proceeding under FOIA from forcing disclosure of a certified photograph, though the government may still release them voluntarily.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary citizens, journalists, and historians lose access to the visual record of how the U.S. military treated detainees, and lose the ability to contest that secrecy in court. Transparency groups' interest in accountability bears the cost.
analysis.who_pays_short: Citizens and journalists seeking the record

drawbacks.text: The decision to withhold rests entirely with the Secretary of Defense, and certifications can be renewed indefinitely in three-year increments, so photographs of detainee treatment can be kept from the public permanently, with no judicial or independent review written into the bill.
The bill blocks not only FOIA disclosure but any proceeding under FOIA, meaning even litigants cannot force the release of certified photographs of detainee treatment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated purpose — protecting troops from retaliation — is a real and serious concern, and photographs released to inflame violence abroad could plausibly cause it. But the tool chosen was sweeping: a cabinet secretary, unilaterally and indefinitely (via renewal), could keep photographs of detainee treatment out of the public record, and Congress could never be confident those decisions were about safety rather than embarrassment. The bill also blocked courts, not just FOIA requesters, from forcing disclosure. That trade came at the expense of the public's ability to know what its government did in its name.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed it without a single recorded vote on the day it was introduced, but it then sat in two House committees until the Congress ended, so it never became law.

narrative.text: The bill passed the Senate by unanimous consent on June 17, 2009, the same day it was introduced, meaning no senator demanded a recorded vote on a measure that would suppress evidence of detainee treatment.
The House referred it to the Oversight and Government Reform and Armed Services committees on June 18, 2009, and neither committee ever acted on it.
The bill died at the end of the 111th Congress in January 2011 without ever receiving a House vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, FOIA requesters, journalists, and litigants retained access to the courts as a route to obtain photographs of detainee treatment, and the Pentagon's authority over that record was never codified.

for.name: Sen. Joseph Lieberman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on June 17, 2009.

for.name: The Senate by unanimous consent
for.what_they_did: Passed the bill without amendment on the day it was introduced, with no recorded vote.

for.name: House Oversight and Government Reform and Armed Services Committees
for.what_they_did: Received the bill on June 18, 2009, and never brought it to the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: The Senate cleared the bill by unanimous consent, so no recorded party split exists; the single recorded cosponsor was a Republican, and the House never voted.

industries.industry: The Defense Department and intelligence community
industries.note: The bill shields images of military and intelligence conduct in detention from public FOIA disclosure and from court challenge, with renewal allowed indefinitely. The military itself is the judge of whether the public may see the record of its own conduct.
